entities.summary:
Oronce Finé (1494–1555) was a pivotal French mathematician, cartographer, and instrument maker whose prolific output significantly shaped early modern European scientific discourse and visual representation of the world. Born in Briançon and active primarily in Paris, Finé's work bridged the theoretical advancements of the Renaissance with practical applications, making complex scientific concepts accessible through meticulously illustrated printed books. As the first Regius Professor of Mathematics at the Collège Royal, his influence extended beyond his publications to a generation of students and practitioners across Western Europe, positioning him as a central figure in the intellectual ferment of the 16th century.

Finé’s most celebrated contributions include his innovative cartographic works, such as the double cordiform (heart-shaped) world map of 1531, which, despite its inherent distortions, became iconic and was widely copied, notably by Mercator. His numerous treatises, including *Protomathesis* (1532) and *De mundi sphaera* (1542), covered a vast array of subjects from arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy to gnomonics (the art of sundial making) and instrument construction. Through his collaboration with leading Parisian printers like Simon de Colines and Robert Estienne, Finé's works, distinguished by their clarity and elegant woodcut illustrations, became standard texts for mathematical education and practical applications across the continent.

entities.summary:
Oronce Finé was a French mathematician, cartographer, editor and book illustrator who played a pivotal role in the development of Renaissance-era cartography. Born in Briançon on December 29, 1494, Finé went on to become one of the most prominent mapmakers of his time, creating detailed and accurate maps of Western Europe and beyond. His work was widely acclaimed by his contemporaries, including the French king Francis I, who sought out Finé's expertise for his own cartographic projects.

Finé's contributions extended far beyond the realm of cartography, however, as he also worked extensively in the fields of mathematics, editing, and book illustration. His mathematical treatises on topics such as optics and perspective were highly influential among the intellectual circles of 16th-century France, while his work on editing and book design helped establish a new standard for scholarly publishing.

Despite his many achievements, Finé's legacy was somewhat overshadowed by that of his more famous contemporaries. Nonetheless, his contributions to the development of Renaissance-era cartography remain an important chapter in the story of European exploration and discovery.

One lasting testament to Finé's enduring impact can be seen in the numerous maps that he created during his lifetime, many of which are now held in archives and museums around Europe. These maps provide a fascinating window into the knowledge and understanding of the time period, offering insights into the geography, politics, and culture of 16th-century Western Europe.
